subject: Biochemistry
vignette: A 55-year-old man is in the third day of a prolonged fast during a hospitalization for pancreatitis. His plasma glucose is maintained at 68 mg/dL, his urine contains ketones, and his liver takes up lactate, alanine, and glycerol to sustain gluconeogenesis. He is not receiving any nutritional supplements.
question: Which of the following substrates can undergo net conversion to glucose in this patient?

options.text: Heptadecanoate (margaric acid), a 17-carbon saturated fatty acid

explanation_correct: Odd-chain fatty acids such as heptadecanoate are oxidized to propionyl-CoA, which is carboxylated to methylmalonyl-CoA with biotin and converted by vitamin B12-dependent methylmalonyl-CoA mutase to succinyl-CoA; succinyl-CoA enters the TCA cycle and can be used for gluconeogenesis. Even-chain fatty acids yield only acetyl-CoA, which cannot produce net glucose in humans, and leucine is purely ketogenic.

explanation_incorrect.A: Palmitate is an even-chain fatty acid that yields acetyl-CoA only; acetyl-CoA cannot be converted to oxaloacetate in humans, so it provides no net glucose.
explanation_incorrect.B: Oleate is also an even-chain fatty acid and yields only acetyl-CoA equivalents, which are ketogenic.
explanation_incorrect.C: Acetoacetate is a ketone body produced by the liver; it is used as fuel by extrahepatic tissues and cannot be converted to glucose.
explanation_incorrect.E: Leucine is one of the two purely ketogenic amino acids (with lysine); it yields acetyl-CoA and acetoacetate but no glucose.

educationalObjective: Odd-chain fatty acids are the only fatty acids that can serve as a net source of glucose, because propionyl-CoA enters the TCA cycle as succinyl-CoA, whereas even-chain fatty acids yield only acetyl-CoA.
